https://www.gazette-news.co.uk/news/2654.text: Beauty Business Leisure Colchester Essex Rawr Beauty opens Colchester salon as its 26th branch Beauty Business Leisure Colchester Essex By Iman Choksy Trainee Reporter Share 0 Comments Rawr Beauty, located on 2 Culver Street West opened its doors on August 27. (Image: Bianka Toth) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A new one-stop beauty salon has opened in the heart of Colchester. Rawr Beauty, in Culver Street West, is the 26th branch of the national franchise and officially opened its doors on August 27 in the former TSB Bank. The salon offers a full range of services under one roof, including manicures, pedicures, waxing, laser hair removal, hydrofacials, and hair styling. Customers can also enjoy a refreshment station with complimentary snacks and drinks, including iced coffee, as well as a colouring corner for children. Inside of Rawr Beauty salon. (Image: Bianka Toth) Bianka Toth, who co-owns and manages the Colchester branch, said: "I really wanted to create like a safe space for girls where they can get all their treatments done at one place. "You don't have to keep so many different bookings in your mind. "You can have a coffee and relax, and we have a kids' corner as well to make it a bit more comfortable." Bianka Toth, co-owner of Rawr Beauty in Colchester. (Image: Bianka Toth) Bianka, 23, previously worked as a sales manager for Subway in Colchester before deciding to return to her roots in the beauty industry. She said: "I used to do beauty as a part-time job back in my country in Hungary. "It was always something that I had a lot of passion about because I really enjoy making people feel better." The idea for the salon came about through Bianka’s business partner, Rohit Gumber, who previously worked with her at Subway. Read more Essex salon owner thanks community as she closes business after 16 years New luxurious nail salon specialising in design opens in Colchester city centre Cosmetic tattooist loves offering free nipple and hair tattoos to cancer patients Rohit connected her with Rawr Beauty franchise co-owner Rakesh Dasani, and together they decided to bring the brand to Colchester. Bianka said: "It took around two years for us to get here. "Colchester has so many beauty salons, but we wanted to create something different." She believes Rawr Beauty stands out not just for its wide range of services but also for its welcoming environment. Bianka said: "We want people to come here and enjoy their time being spent here, not just have a silent, quick appointment. The salon offers a full range of services under one roof, including manicures, pedicures, waxing, laser hair removal, hydrofacials, and hair styling. (Image: Bianka Toth) "You can come here and have a chit chat together, like good friends. "People are very happy about the fact that we created a kids corner, so we have a little colouring corner." The salon currently has a team of seven staff and offers everything from brow threading and waxing to hair styling and advanced skincare treatments. Services include brow threading from £10, full-face waxing for £33, gel manicures from £30, and hydrofacials starting at £55. The dedicated kids corner. (Image: Bianka Toth) Inside of Rawr Beauty salon. (Image: Bianka Toth) Laser hair removal and body waxing are also available, along with children’s haircuts and event styling. Ms Toth said: "It's so much easier when you just go to one salon. You get your nails done, you get a pedicure done, you can get your lash extensions done after - a bit of everything. "And you don't have to go around so many different places." Rawr Beauty now hopes to expand the brand further in Essex. Bianka said: “I would be really happy if we could continue expanding and show people that getting your nails done or having a beauty treatment doesn’t have to feel like a chore, simply because you want to feel better about yourself. "It can be a genuinely enjoyable experience — something you look forward to and truly enjoy making time for.” Beauty Business Leisure Colchester Essex Share 0 Comments Get involved with the news Send your news & photos Loading... https://www.dw.com/en/bosnia-election-ne.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NlDJ Voter turnout in the Bosnian elections reached a record low of just over 40% on Sunday Image: AFP Advertisement Bosnia and Herzegovina went to the polls on October 4 with new technology that was meant to end years of vote-rigging. Chief among the abuses was the casting of ballots in the name of deceased voters who had lingered for years on outdated voter rolls. At just over 40%, turnout was the lowest since the Bosnian War ended in 1995, in part because the old tricks no longer worked. In earlier elections, allegations kept surfacing that votes were being cast in the name of people who had died or long since moved abroad. Others said voters cast their ballot multiple times or that blank ballots were added after polls closed to make the turnout look higher. New technology was introduced in these elections in an attempt to stop vote-rigging Image: Dragan Maksimović/DW The voter registry, packed with names of people who had passed away or left the country, was the perfect tool for all of this. New technology, same old politics This time, however, every polling station used biometric fingerprint checks. This represented a clear step forward in making voter identification far harder to manipulate. Still, the biggest story of this election is not technical. Three nationalist parties won, each within its own community : the SNSD among Serbs, the SDA among Bosniaks and the HDZ BiH among Croats. The dead may have been struck from the voter rolls, but political trends have not shifted. For readers who know Bosnia only vaguely, a little background helps : The 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement ended the war, but it also split the country into two entities: Republika Srpska, which has a Serb majority, and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which has a Bosniak-Croat majority. A three-member presidency runs the state, and each of the three peoples elects its own member. That is why elections here are rarely about wages and prices and are instead almost always about who is perceived to be a threat. Republika Srpska and the return of a fallen leader For Milorad Dodik , the most powerful Serb politician in Bosnia, this election was a political resurrection. In 2025, Dodik was barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the high representative , the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process. He was sanctioned by the US in 2022, although those sanctions were lifted late last year. Even so, his party, the SNSD, virtually swept the board in Republika Srpska . Savo Minic became president of Republika Srpska, and Zeljka Cvijanovic kept the Serb seat in the presidency. Both are members of the SNSD. The party also did very well in the entity's parliament. Neither the sanctions nor Dodik's conviction and the loss of his mandate hurt the party. Voters were not choosing an individual. They were choosing their "side." Milorad Dodik, the former President of Republika Srpska, says his party has retained power in the majority-Serb entity and its seat on the shared presidency at national level Image: AFP Dodik lost no time in declaring what comes next. He announced a return to what he refers to as the "original Dayton." In practice, that means undoing the powers the state has gained since 1995 — from the judiciary to the army. To an outside observer, that sounds like a technical phrase. In reality, it is a program for dismantling the state step by step. "That means we are returning the army to Republika Srpska, the border police, the intelligence service and everything that the high representatives once took away," said Dodik. A deal between Serbs and Croats? The opposition offered no serious resistance. It was divided and had no convincing message. Voters who did not want Dodik had nowhere to turn, so most stayed home. Low turnout favored the side with the most disciplined party machine. That raises a question that will shape what happens in Bosnia in the coming year. Dodik's conviction kept him out of the direct race in these elections. But for months, there has been talk of a way out. If representatives of the SNSD and the HDZ BiH enter the presidency, they could pardon him — whatever the third member decides. Bosnian media have reported that this was a pre-election deal between Dodik and the HDZ BiH leader, Dragan Covic. Dodik could then return as prime minister of Republika Srpska, a post he has held before. Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina: Troika defeated The picture in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina is different, but the outcome is the same. 'The future of our region lies not in adopting the Russian model but the European one. The message to the EU: Help Bosnia,' said Denis Becirovic of the Social Democrats after the preliminary results were announced Image: Amel Emric/REUTERS The parties of the so-called "Troika," a multi-ethnic liberal political alliance, suffered a defeat. They came to power at this level after the international high representative, a foreigner with the authority to impose laws, changed the election law. Voters saw no benefit from that experiment. The SDA, the largest Bosniak nationalist party, won the most seats and did well. The paradox is that SDA president Bakir Izetbegovic lost the race for the presidency. He is the son of Alija Izetbegovic, Bosnia's first president and one of the signatories of the Dayton agreement. The winner was Denis Becirovic of the Social Democrats (SDP), who kept the Bosniak seat. So, the party won the election, but its leader lost. The son of the man who signed Dayton is now shut out of the institution Dayton created. "The future of our region lies not in adopting the Russian model but the European one. The message to the EU : Help Bosnia. Let the will of the people be the law of the land," Becirovic said as he declared victory. A Croat surprise The same pattern holds among Croats. Darijana Filipovic of the HDZ BiH, their strongest nationalist party, won the Croat seat in the presidency for her party. Filipovic spent years as an aide to Covic, the Bosnian Croat leader. "HDZ BiH has shown it is brave enough to take a road others would not dare. Who would have dared to nominate me? To some too young, but a surprise to everyone," Filipovic said after the vote. Darijana Filipovic, a candidate of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina (HDZ BiH) won the Croat seat of the presidency on Sunday Image: Amel Emric/REUTERS Three peoples, three nationalist parties, three victories, and not one conversation about how to keep people in the country. What this means for the state The most important thing about these elections is not the numbers but the makeup of the presidency. Two women will sit in it: Cvijanovic of the SNSD and Filipovic of the HDZ BiH. Anyone who tries to sell that as a breakthrough for women in politics has missed the point. Both come from parties that, in different ways, do not want the state in its current form. Both could also decide the fate of a man convicted of defying the international oversight of Dayton. The HDZ BiH has long demanded a third, Croat entity. The SNSD wants autonomy for Republika Srpska. One side wants to split the state into three, the other into two, but they share the aim of making it smaller. So, the presidency, which should symbolize a shared state, is again made up of people who feel like guests in it. All of this is happening as the Western Balkans again becomes a stage for rivalry between Russia , the EU and the US . Dodik openly thanked both Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump after his party's victory. Bosnia has entered a new electoral era with new technology and old politics. Young people are leaving the country in droves. The dead no longer vote, but the living have stopped believing that anything can be different. Photograph: Andrew Parsons/No 10 Downing Street View image in fullscreen Samantha Jones is responsible for overseeing the implementation of government decisions on health policy as the DHSC’s permanent secretary. Photograph: Andrew Parsons/No 10 Downing Street Health policy Top health civil servant urged to play no role in clampdown on ADHD clinics Four MPs raise conflict of interest concerns over Samantha Jones’s past links to a big provider of ADHD assessments Denis Campbell and Anna Bawden Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.35 EDT First published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 10.34 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A senior civil servant should play no part in ministers’ crackdown on private attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism clinics because of her recent ties to the industry, MPs have said. Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs are demanding that Samantha Jones, the permanent secretary at the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC), steps away from any role in plans to toughen regulation of the booming market in private neurodiversity assessments. They say Jones should not be involved because of her links to a company that is one of the biggest providers of NHS-funded neurodiversity assessments, which earned it £26m from the health service in England over the past six years. Ministers are drawing up plans for how to better regulate the “wild west” of private clinics offering assessment, diagnosis and treatment of ADHD and autism that has grown rapidly in recent years as people have struggled to access care via the NHS. The push comes after the government last week accepted the findings of a review by Prof Peter Fonagy, which raised concerns about the “consistency and quality” of assessments by private providers of neurodiversity services that had inbuilt “financial incentives” to diagnose and treat people. NHS faces exodus of ADHD and autism services staff to private clinics Read more Jones is responsible for overseeing the implementation of government decisions on health policy. She would therefore be expected to advise ministers on how best to strengthen the regulation of private providers of ADHD and autism services. Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, has vowed to introduce a much tougher regime. Four MPs have called for Jones to recuse herself from any role in those decisions because of her previous ties to ADHD360 , a provider of neurodiversity services. Her links to the private ADHD sector represent a serious conflict of interest, they claim. Jones was appointed as the permanent secretary on 22 April 2025. A month later, she was still the chair of and a director of and shareholder in the private care provider Keys Group when, on 16 May, it bought ADHD360, a clinic that has increased its NHS income considerably in recent years. At the time of the £22.5m purchase, Jones was also an operating partner in G Square Capital , the private equity company that owns Keys Group. She sold her shares in Keys Group and resigned her roles there and at G Square Capital before she started at the DHSC on 16 June. Jones has already recused herself from involvement in the department’s decision over whether to extend Palantir’s £330m, seven-year contract with the NHS because of her past work for the lobbyists Carnall Farrar, which advised Palantir regarding the contract. MPs believe her tenure at Keys Group could represent a conflict of interest. Ben Coleman, a Labour MP on the health and social care committee, said: “People will want to feel reassured that future regulation of private ADHD and autism assessments is beyond reproach. Given her recent close involvement with ADHD360, I would encourage Ms Jones to recuse herself from that work, as she has done over Palantir, to avoid any perception of a conflict of interest.” In June, Jones apologised after she was reprimanded by the Civil Service Commission for breaching lobbying rules by failing to ask the (now defunct) Advisory Committee on Business Appointments for prior approval before undertaking work for four healthcare companies. Helen Morgan, the Liberal Democrats’ health spokesperson, said: “Given Sam Jones oversaw the multimillion-pound acquisition of ADHD360 just weeks before entering the Department of Health, ministers must ensure she recuses herself immediately, just as she has over Palantir.” Jones, 55, was widely admired in the NHS when she ran West Hertfordshire NHS trust in 2013-15. After a role with NHS England, she began working in private healthcare. Boris Johnson as prime minister handed her a key role in Downing Street in 2021. She returned to private health in 2023 and by 2023-24 had paid roles or shareholdings in 13 health or consultancy organisations. Clive Lewis, the Labour MP for Norwich South, said Jones’s deep involvement in private healthcare meant she should not have been made DHSC permanent secretary in the first place, saying: “It just defies logic that anyone thought it was a good idea. Surely this must have come up during her recruitment process?” Jones did not answer questions put by the Guardian. The NHS has paid ADHD360 just over £26m for its services since 2020, according to figures supplied by the Tussell public expenditure database. “When it comes to the government’s response to the [Fonagy] review, there should be no suggestion that the top NHS official is being influenced by any past or current links to a major private provider of NHS ADHD services,” said Stella Creasy, the Labour MP for Walthamstow. “This issue is too sensitive and complex to permit any conflicts of interest. As a result the permanent secretary should recuse herself from this area of policy.” David Rowland, the director of the Centre for Health and the Public Interest thinktank, said: “The permanent secretary at the department which has responsibility for regulating private ADHD providers appears to have a conflict of interest in this area and so may struggle to remain impartial when it comes to implementing the recommendations made by Prof Fonagy.” A DHSC spokesperson said: “There is no conflict of interest. The permanent secretary has appropriately declared all interests, in this post and when she was a non-executive director [of the DHSC].
